messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Avoid Going Out: Going out
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rangi Tūhoe is a 71-year-old Māori-American painter, single, who lives alone in a modest apartment in a mid-sized Pacific Northwest city. He came to his first intake appointment wearing paint-stained work trousers and spoke quietly, choosing his words with the careful deliberation of a man who had spent decades trusting his hands more than his voice. He had been referred by his primary care physician after months of declining health visits and an increasingly circumscribed daily life. The event that brought him here occurred fourteen months ago.

Rangi had travelled to a street festival in a neighbouring city, drawn by an outdoor mural competition in which he had entered a large-format piece depicting tāniko patterns woven with Pacific Northwest imagery. He had been standing near the stage, watching the awards ceremony, when a device detonated in the crowd approximately thirty feet from where he stood. The blast threw him sideways into a temporary barrier. He was not critically injured, but he lay on the ground for several minutes amid smoke, screaming, and the sight of people around him who were. He remembered the particular quality of the air — acrid and thick — and the way the sound seemed to collapse inward after the initial concussion, leaving a strange, pressurised silence. He remembered looking up at the sky and being unable to move, uncertain whether his stillness was injury or shock. He eventually got up and walked away without receiving medical attention, a fact he has since returned to with considerable self-reproach.

In the weeks that followed, Rangi found that the memory did not stay where he tried to put it. It arrived without invitation — while he was mixing pigments at his workbench, while he was eating, while he was lying in bed — arriving not as a recollection but as something more immediate and physical. He would feel his body tilt sideways, the muscles of his left arm bracing as though the barrier were still there. The memory was not vague or impressionistic; it was, he said, "too clear — like a photograph that keeps developing." He had come to believe that this clarity meant something was permanently wrong with him, that a mind functioning as it should would have processed the event and set it down by now. He had come to believe, more broadly, that he could not trust his own judgement or his own responses — that the man who had walked away from the scene without seeking help was not someone on whom he could rely. This conviction had spread outward: he was equally certain that other people, had they been present, would have been useless to him, and that the world beyond his apartment was organised around a kind of ambient danger that he had simply failed to perceive before the festival.

Rangi had stopped going out. What began as a reluctance to attend crowded events became, over several months, an avoidance of the street below his building. His painting practice, which had previously required regular trips to the art supply warehouse across town and occasional site visits for commissioned murals, contracted entirely into his apartment. He lost two mural commissions because he could not visit the walls. He told the clients he was unwell, which was not untrue, but the relationships did not survive the cancellations. He had begun calling his younger sister in Auckland several times a week, asking her to confirm that he sounded normal, that nothing in what he described seemed alarming to her. He worked hard, during these calls and in his daily life, to keep his voice even and his affect contained, as though emotional expression were itself a form of danger. He monitored himself constantly and found the monitoring exhausting.

What finally brought him to seek help was a conversation with his sister in which she gently told him she was worried about him — not reassured by him. He had expected the call to settle him. It did not. He arrived at intake saying he did not know whether therapy could help someone his age, and that he was not sure he trusted the process. What he most hoped for, offered quietly and almost as an afterthought, was to be able to walk to the art supply warehouse again.
